results.title: Researcher affirms human creativity's value amid AI - Tech Xplore
results.content: Recent research co-authored by Kaufman, along with his new edited scholarly volume on generative AI and creativity, suggests that while artificial intelligence can support some aspects of creative work, it does not replace human creativity. "Most creativity researchers tend to fall into two camps, those who are very excited about AI and those who are deeply concerned about it," Kaufman says. Working across disciplines, Worwood says one of the most surprising aspects of the project was the range of perspectives contributors brought to discussions of generative AI and creativity. That diversity, Worwood says, reinforces the book's central argument that AI should be treated as a tool rather than a replacement for human creativity, particularly in educational settings. For educators, policymakers, and creative professionals, the challenge is not whether to engage with AI, but how to do so without sacrificing learning, equity, and human judgment. Generative AI can assist creative work but does not replace human creativity; it amplifies existing differences in skill and judgment.

results.content: [Skip to content](https://news.ucsc.edu/2026/01/shaping-the-future-of-artificial-intelligence/#wp--skip-link--target). [Yi Zhang](https://campusdirectory.ucsc.edu/cd_detail?uid=yiz), the director of the [UC Santa Cruz Generative AI Center](https://genai.ucsc.edu/) and professor of computer science and engineering, is a veteran of the AI field, having been involved from both the academic and industry founder sides for many years. Assistant Professor of Computer Science and Engineering [Leilani Gilpin](https://campusdirectory.ucsc.edu/cd_detail?uid=lgilpin)’s [AI Explainability and Accountability Lab](https://aiea-lab.github.io/) is developing and evaluating methods for different kinds of AI models—from chatbots to autonomous vehicles—to explain their behavior. Associate Professor of Literature [Zac Zimmer](https://campusdirectory.ucsc.edu/cd_detail?uid=zaazimme) is an expert in digital humanities who has studied how human creativity intersects with AI infrastructures, especially regarding data use, training, and intellectual property, and the nature of the data used to train AI systems. He participated in curating the Exploratorium’s [Adventures in AI](https://www.exploratorium.edu/visit/calendar/ai) exhibition and teaches LIT 126H: _Artificial Intelligence and Human Imagination_, a course designed as part of the [Responsible Artificial Intelligence Curriculum Design Project](https://news.ucsc.edu/2022/06/responsible-ai/) from the National Humanities Center.

results.title: AI can spark creativity — if we ask it how, not what, to think - Nature
results.content: # AI can spark creativity — if we ask it how, not what, to think. Studies aiming to maximize human creativity demonstrate that people work best when buoyed up by others who show them new ways to innovate. However, in practice, the opposite is often true — bots flatten creativity. Can AI be truly creative? As a researcher who has spent 30 years studying human creativity, I think I know why. When a scientist feeds a data set into a bot and says “give me hypotheses to test”, they are asking the bot to be the creator, not a creative partner. Instead, researchers should learn how to use bots to boost their creativity. I’ve been working with a test of rapid creative thinking called the divergent association task (DAT), which I think points to a way forwards. Work on human creativity backs up this idea. * Can AI be truly creative? * #### Tenure-track Faculty Positions in Theoretical Particle Physics and Cosmology.
